items.prompt: State what is meant by phagocytosis.
items.canonical_answer: Phagocytosis is the engulfing of a pathogen by a cell, which encloses it in a vesicle and digests it with enzymes.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition names engulfing a pathogen and breaking it down with enzymes (lysosomes accepted). The key words are engulf and digest. Engulfing with no digestion, or killing with no idea of taking the pathogen in, does not earn the mark.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: State the part of a phagocyte that fuses with the vesicle holding an engulfed bacterium and releases digestive enzymes into it.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the part is the lysosome (lysosomes accepted). Its function is to release hydrolytic enzymes that digest the bacterium. Golgi apparatus is rejected, because it makes lysosomes but does not fuse with the vesicle to digest the contents; ribosome and mitochondrion are rejected.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: A learner writes that after a macrophage has engulfed a bacterium, it 'shows loose fragments of the bacterium to the T-helper cell'. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is to picture loose fragments being shown. In fact the macrophage places antigens from the bacterium on its own cell surface membrane, so that they are held in the membrane. A T-helper cell with a complementary receptor binds to these antigens. The test is to ask what exactly sits on the macrophage's membrane: the answer is antigens from the pathogen, in the membrane of the macrophage itself.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that loose fragments are displayed instead of antigens in the macrophage's membrane (1); the correct idea, antigens from the pathogen placed on the macrophage's own surface membrane, or the test question that separates the two (1).
The card is a discrimination between the two ideas, not a repeat of the definition of phagocytosis.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt:
These are our blood counts for a farm worker near Tsumeb who had a bacterial infection in a cut on his leg.

| Day after the infection began | Neutrophils in the blood (cells per mm³) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 4100 |
| 1 | 9800 |
| 2 | 13200 |
| 4 | 7000 |
| 7 | 4300 |

Describe the change in the number of neutrophils, and say what it means for the phagocytes at the infection.
items.canonical_answer: The count rises from 4100 cells per mm³ at day 0 to a peak of 13200 cells per mm³ at day 2, then falls to 4300 cells per mm³ by day 7. The rise means that more phagocytes are in the blood, available to move into the infected tissue and engulf and digest the bacteria. The fall shows that the infection is being cleared, so fewer are needed.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the table read with values and units, a rise to a peak of 13200 cells per mm³ at day 2 and a fall to 4300 cells per mm³ by day 7 (1); the data means more phagocytes are available to engulf bacteria at the infection, and the later fall shows the infection clearing (1).
Both readings must come from the table. A statement that the neutrophils make antibodies is rejected.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: Describe the sequence of events in a primary immune response, from the engulfing of a bacterium by a macrophage to the secretion of antibodies. [3]
items.canonical_answer: A macrophage engulfs and digests the bacterium and presents its antigens on its own surface membrane. A T-helper cell with a complementary receptor binds to the presented antigen, divides to form a clone and releases cytokines. These stimulate a B-lymphocyte whose receptors fit the antigen, which divides into plasma cells and memory cells, and the plasma cells secrete antibodies.
marking_guidance: 3 marks from the points, in this order: macrophage presents antigens on its own surface membrane (1); T-helper cell binds, divides and releases cytokines (1); B-lymphocyte stimulated and divides into plasma cells (1); plasma cells secrete antibodies (end product). Four points are creditworthy, so the cap is 3 marks.
The sequence must be in order: antibodies before the T-helper step, or T-helper cells before the macrophage, is not credited as a stage in the right place.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: Describe how T-helper cells lead to the secretion of antibodies by plasma cells. [2]
items.canonical_answer: A T-helper cell that has bound the antigen presented on a macrophage divides and releases cytokines. These chemical signals stimulate a B-lymphocyte with a matching receptor to divide, and the cells of this clone become plasma cells, which then secrete antibodies.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from three points: the T-helper cell releases cytokines (chemical signals) (1); which cause a B-lymphocyte with a matching receptor to divide or clone (1); the cells become plasma cells, which secrete antibodies, so antibody follows from the signal (1). The cap is 2 marks.
Credit how the signal leads to the antibody, not a restatement that T-helper cells help. A T-helper cell that secretes antibodies itself is rejected.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: A rare condition in a patient in Windhoek means that her blood contains no T-helper cells, although her B-lymphocytes and macrophages are normal. Explain why she makes very few antibodies when bacteria infect her. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Without T-helper cells there are no cytokines to stimulate the B-lymphocytes, because the macrophages present antigens but no T-helper cell exists to bind them and respond. So few B-lymphocytes divide into plasma cells, and there are few plasma cells to secrete antibodies.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from three points: no T-helper cells to bind the antigen presented by the macrophages, so the response does not start (1); no cytokines, so the B-lymphocytes are not stimulated to divide (1); few plasma cells, therefore few antibodies (1). The cap is 2 marks.
The answer must be about this patient's case, with normal B-lymphocytes and macrophages, and must give a cause-and-effect chain, not state that her immunity is weak.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: A learner writes: 'When a B-lymphocyte clones, it makes many antibodies, which are new cells that attack the pathogen.' Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is to treat antibodies as cells made by cloning. In fact a B-lymphocyte clones into plasma cells and memory cells, and it is the plasma cells that secrete antibodies, which are protein molecules, not cells. The test is to ask which cell makes antibodies and what an antibody is: a plasma cell makes them, and an antibody is a protein.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the error named, that antibodies are treated as cells produced by cloning (1); the correct idea, that B-lymphocytes clone into plasma cells and memory cells and plasma cells secrete antibodies, which are proteins, or the test question that separates them (1).
The card is a discrimination, not a repeat of the definition of an antibody.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt:
These are our values for a patient in the first 15 days after infection with a bacterium.

| Day | Plasma cells in the blood (cells per mm³) | Antibody concentration (arbitrary units) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 15 | 0 |
| 6 | 420 | 8 |
| 9 | 1350 | 55 |
| 12 | 600 | 90 |
| 15 | 150 | 70 |

Describe the pattern in the table, and say what it means about how plasma cells and antibody are related.
items.canonical_answer: The number of plasma cells rises to a peak of 1350 cells per mm³ at day 9 and then falls, whereas the antibody concentration peaks later, at 90 arbitrary units at day 12. This means that antibody is made by the plasma cells and builds up in the blood, so its concentration follows the plasma cell count after a delay. The lack of antibody at day 3 shows that a lag is needed first for the response to build.
marking_guidance: 2 marks: the table read with values, plasma cells peak at 1350 cells per mm³ at day 9 and antibody peaks later at 90 arbitrary units at day 12 (1); the data means that plasma cells make the antibody, so antibody follows plasma cells after a delay while it builds up (1).
A reading from one column only earns the first mark only if the peak is named with its day and unit.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by an antigen.
items.canonical_answer: An antigen is a molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein, on the surface of a cell or pathogen that triggers an immune response.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition has three key words, a molecule, on the surface of a cell or pathogen, and triggers an immune response. Antibody is rejected, because an antibody is a protein made by plasma cells, not the molecule that triggers the response.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: State the difference between a self antigen and a non-self antigen.
items.canonical_answer: A self antigen is on the body's own cells and does not normally trigger an immune response, whereas a non-self antigen is not part of the body, for example one on a pathogen, and triggers a response.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: both sides of the difference, self antigens on the body's own cells, whereas non-self antigens are foreign, as on pathogens, and trigger a response. A statement about one side alone does not earn the mark.
Reject any answer that places self antigens on pathogens, or that says the difference is the type of molecule.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: State what is meant by a memory cell.
items.canonical_answer: A memory cell is a long-lived cell formed when lymphocytes clone in the primary immune response, which stays in the body and responds quickly if the same antigen is met again.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the definition has two key words, long-lived cell that remains in the body after the primary response, and a quick response to the same antigen again. A cell that secretes antibody during the primary response describes a plasma cell and is rejected.
items.provenance: Authored for topic 2.9.1 from the topic claim ledger. Unverified.

items.prompt: Explain why the secondary immune response to an antigen is faster and produces more antibody than the primary response. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Memory cells formed in the primary response remain in the body, so there are many more cells that match the antigen than before. They are stimulated quickly when the antigen returns and divide rapidly into plasma cells, which secrete large amounts of antibody sooner.
marking_guidance: 2 marks from three points: memory cells from the primary response remain, so many more cells match the antigen (1); they are stimulated quickly and divide rapidly (1); into plasma cells, which result in more antibody sooner (1). The cap is 2 marks.
The answer must give the cause, not repeat that the response is faster.

items.prompt:
Twelve questions. Choose one option for each.

1. Which part of a phagocyte releases hydrolytic enzymes into the vesicle holding an engulfed bacterium?
A  a ribosome
B  a lysosome
C  the nucleus
D  a mitochondrion

2. Where are antigens from a pathogen placed when a macrophage presents them to a T-helper cell?
A  free in the cytoplasm of the macrophage
B  inside the vesicle where the pathogen was digested
C  on the macrophage's own cell surface membrane
D  on the surface membrane of the T-helper cell

3. Which cells secrete antibodies?
A  macrophages
B  T-killer cells
C  plasma cells
D  memory cells

4. Which statement about antibodies is correct?
A  They are cells formed when B-lymphocytes clone.
B  They are protein molecules secreted by plasma cells.
C  They are molecules on the surface of a pathogen that trigger a response.
D  They are cells that engulf pathogens.

5. Which statement gives the difference between self antigens and non-self antigens?
A  Self antigens are on the body's own cells, whereas non-self antigens are on pathogens or other foreign cells.
B  Self antigens trigger an immune response, whereas non-self antigens do not.
C  Self antigens are proteins, whereas non-self antigens are carbohydrates.
D  Self antigens are on the surface of cells, whereas non-self antigens are inside cells.

6. What is the role of a T-killer cell?
A  It secretes antibodies into the blood plasma.
B  It engulfs bacteria and presents their antigens.
C  It releases signals that stimulate B-lymphocytes to divide.
D  It destroys body cells that are infected and display a non-self antigen.

7. A farm worker has a bacterial infection in a wound, and his blood count shows a high number of neutrophils. What does this most likely mean?
A  Plasma cells are already secreting large amounts of antibody.
B  More phagocytes are available to move to the wound and engulf the bacteria.
C  Memory cells have destroyed the bacteria.
D  T-killer cells are engulfing the bacteria.

8. A bacterium carries antigen Z. A person has B-lymphocytes with receptors that fit antigen Y and others with receptors that fit antigen Z. Which statement is correct?
A  Both sets of B-lymphocytes divide, because the bacterium is non-self.
B  The B-lymphocytes with receptors that fit Y are selected, because they were made first.
C  The B-lymphocytes with receptors that fit Z can bind the bacterium and are selected to divide when stimulated.
D  The B-lymphocytes with receptors that fit Y secrete antibodies that fit Z.

9. Four events in a primary immune response are: P, a B-lymphocyte divides to form plasma cells and memory cells; Q, a macrophage presents antigens on its surface membrane; R, plasma cells secrete antibodies; S, a T-helper cell binds the antigen and releases signals. Which sequence is correct?
A  Q, S, P, R
B  S, Q, P, R
C  Q, S, R, P
D  P, Q, S, R

10. Which statement about memory cells is correct?
A  They secrete large amounts of antibody during the primary response.
B  They destroy body cells that are infected.
C  They die when the pathogen has been destroyed, so the next response is as slow as the first.
D  They remain in the body for years and divide rapidly into plasma cells if the same antigen is met again.

11. A girl in Opuwo recovered from measles when she was six. At fifteen she is exposed to the measles virus again and does not become ill. Which explanation is best?
A  The plasma cells from the first infection are still secreting antibody at the highest concentration.
B  Memory cells from the first infection quickly divide into plasma cells, which secrete antibody before the virus can multiply enough to cause symptoms.
C  Her neutrophils remember the virus and engulf it faster.
D  The virus is now a self antigen, so her body needs no response.

12. Our table gives values from one patient who met the same antigen twice.

| Exposure | Days before antibody was first detected | Peak antibody concentration (arbitrary units) |
|---|---|---|
| first | 7 | 40 |
| second | 2 | 280 |

Which conclusion does the table support?
A  The response to the second exposure starts sooner and reaches a higher peak.
B  The response to the second exposure starts later but reaches a higher peak.
C  The response to the second exposure starts sooner but reaches the same peak.
D  The two responses are the same, because the antigen is the same.
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 C, 3 C, 4 B, 5 A, 6 D, 7 B, 8 C, 9 A, 10 D, 11 B, 12 A.
1. Lysosomes fuse with the vesicle and release enzymes that digest the bacterium. (B) A: a ribosome makes proteins and does not digest an engulfed pathogen. C: the nucleus holds the DNA and does not release digestive enzymes. D: a mitochondrion releases energy in respiration and does not digest the contents of a vesicle.
2. The antigens are held in the macrophage's surface membrane, where a T-helper cell can bind them. (C) A: antigens free in the cytoplasm cannot be bound by a receptor on another cell. B: this confuses digestion with presentation, since a T-helper cell cannot reach the inside of a vesicle. D: this reverses the direction, because the T-helper cell binds the antigen on the macrophage.
3. Plasma cells are the cells that secrete antibodies. (C) A: macrophages present antigens and do not secrete antibody. B: T-killer cells destroy infected body cells. D: memory cells stay in the body ready for a later response and do not secrete antibody in the primary response.
4. Antibodies are proteins, secreted by plasma cells. (B) A: this is the register error of treating antibodies as cells; B-lymphocytes clone into plasma cells and memory cells. C: this describes antigens, a near-neighbour term. D: this describes phagocytes, which are cells.
5. The difference is one of origin: own cells against foreign cells and pathogens. (A) B: this reverses the two, because non-self antigens trigger the response. C: the difference is origin, not the chemical type of the molecule. D: both kinds are on surfaces and the difference is not position.
6. T-killer cells destroy infected body cells that display the antigen. (D) A: this is the role of a plasma cell. B: this is the role of a macrophage. C: this is the role of a T-helper cell, a near-neighbour term.
7. Neutrophils are phagocytes, and their number in the blood rises in a bacterial infection. (B) A: neutrophils are not plasma cells and make no antibody. C: memory cells have a role only on a later exposure, and they do not engulf bacteria. D: T-killer cells destroy infected body cells and do not engulf bacteria.
8. Receptors and antibodies are specific, so only the matching lymphocytes are selected. (C) A: this ignores specificity, since a receptor binds one antigen and not another. B: the order of making has no effect on selection; the match decides. D: an antibody fits the antigen its cell was selected by, so this reverses specificity.
9. Presentation comes first, then the T-helper cell, then cloning of the B-lymphocyte, then secretion. (A) B: a T-helper cell cannot bind an antigen that has not yet been presented. C: antibody cannot be secreted before the plasma cells exist. D: the B-lymphocyte is stimulated by the T-helper cell, so it cannot divide first.
10. Memory cells persist and give the quick secondary response. (D) A: this describes plasma cells. B: this describes T-killer cells. C: this ignores the persistence of memory cells, which is the reason the secondary response is faster.
11. The secondary response is quick and large because of memory cells. (B) A: plasma cells are short-lived and the high concentration of the first response does not last for years. C: neutrophils are non-specific phagocytes and keep no memory of an antigen. D: the virus does not become a self antigen, since self antigens are those on the body's own cells.
12. 2 days is shorter than 7 days, and 280 is higher than 40. (A) B: the lag is 2 days against 7 days, so the second response starts sooner. C: the peaks are 280 and 40 arbitrary units, which are not the same. D: the table shows that the two responses differ, because memory cells act in the second.
marking_guidance: The key: one mark per correct option, twelve marks in all; about half the questions test recall and half test application to a described situation, sequence or table.

Each distractor is a named error: antibodies treated as cells, antigen and antibody confused, T-helper and T-killer roles swapped, a macrophage said to hold antigens in its cytoplasm, the steps out of order, memory cells given the work of plasma cells (the misconception register first).

items.prompt:
A patient was infected with bacterium X on day 0 and exposed to the same bacterium again on day 30. These are our values for the concentration of antibody against X in her blood.

| Day | Antibody concentration (arbitrary units) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0 |
| 4 | 0 |
| 8 | 5 |
| 12 | 30 |
| 16 | 45 |
| 20 | 35 |
| 24 | 20 |
| 30 | 15 |
| 32 | 60 |
| 34 | 240 |
| 36 | 300 |
| 40 | 260 |
| 50 | 200 |

(a) State the name of the cells that secrete the antibody. [1]
(b) Describe two differences between the antibody response after day 30 and the response after day 0. [2]
(c) Explain why the response after day 30 is faster. [2]
(d) Suggest why the antibody concentration falls after each peak. [2]
(e) State the name of the molecule on the surface of bacterium X that the antibody binds. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Plasma cells.
(b) After day 30 antibody appears within 2 days, as 60 arbitrary units at day 32, whereas after day 0 it was first detected at day 8 (5 arbitrary units). The peak after day 30 is 300 arbitrary units at day 36, much higher than the peak of 45 arbitrary units at day 16.
(c) Memory cells formed after the first infection remained in the body, so many cells matched the antigen. They were stimulated quickly and divided rapidly into plasma cells, which secrete large amounts of antibody sooner.
(d) Once the bacteria have been destroyed, the antigen no longer stimulates more plasma cells, and plasma cells are short-lived, so less antibody is made. Antibodies are proteins, which are also broken down or removed after binding the bacteria, so the concentration falls.
(e) An antigen.
marking_guidance: Marks and points: (a) 1 mark for plasma cells; (b) 2 marks from four points: shorter lag after day 30 with values, higher peak with values, steeper rise, stays high for longer, each quoted with units where a value is given; (c) 2 marks from three points: memory cells remain, stimulated quickly, divide rapidly into plasma cells.

(d) 2 marks from three points: the antigen is removed so no further stimulation, plasma cells are short-lived, antibodies are broken down or used up; (e) 1 mark for antigen (antibody is rejected). Parts (a) and (e) credit AO A (2 marks); parts (b), (c) and (d) credit AO B (6 marks). The reason in part (c) must be about memory cells, not a general statement that the body has learned.
Reject answers to part (a) that name antibodies or B-lymphocytes as the cells that secrete the antibody; a term from the wrong set is not accepted.
